tone_statements.citation: Bateman, Janet (comp.), with Ananias Tawari, Sakaria Omo, Benjamin Omo & Timotius Tawari. 2020 [created 1980-2020]. Iau - English Dictionary (Iau Lexicon). Data set, 336 pp. (docx) + Lexique Pro database. SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 86738 (posted as is).
tone_statements.quote: Iau is a tonal language. Tone is both lexical and morphemic. . In the Iau phoneme inventory, there are 6 consonants, 8 vowels and 8 phonemic tones. There are no phonemic nasals. But there are nasal allophones of some of the voiced stops. Iau, like other Lakes Plain languages has a high front vowel that is fricativized and implosive voiced stops. (Bateman, 1990)
tone_statements.summary: States Iau is tonal with 8 phonemic tones, tone both lexical and morphemic (citing Bateman 1990); the tones are not named or described by shape here; nothing on word stress.

tone_statements.quote: Iau has 8 phonemic tonesv: 2 contrastive level tones and 6 contrastive contours (3 falling contours, 2 rising contours and 1 fall-rise contour) which are displayed in Figure 1 below. tone_statements.summary: Eight phonemic tones: two level (high, low) and six contours (three falls, two rises, fall-rise), written 2-9; two-tone sequences occur on one syllable; tone is lexical and marks aspect and mood.

tone_statements.quote: The same set of eight basic tone morphemes in Iau which are used on verb stems to indicate aspect and on other post verbal particles to indicate status (Bateman, 1986a, 1986b), are used on illocutionary force particles to indicate both the relationship of the information to discourse topic and the speaker hearer relationship. … A single set of the 8 basic Iau tone morphemes occurs on Iau verbs and on the Iau postverbal particles … On verbs, the tone morphemes indicate 8 contrastive aspectual viewpoints.

tone_statements.summary: Eight basic tones (numbered 2-9) act as morphemes: aspect on verb stems, status on postverbal particles, speaker-hearer pragmatics on final particles; pitch shapes are not described in this article.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant, rule 01 = second/final syllable of disyllables; stress non-lexical, tone carries the contrasts) rests on Bateman 1990 sec. 3.1 p.34, which I downloaded from sealang and confirmed verbatim on the page scan, with the two illustrating forms on p.35 and the word-shape census on p.38 (c. 100 disyllabic nouns in a 3000-word dictionary, rest monosyllabic). This is the primary and only published phonology of Iau, by its principal describer; Glottolog lists no reference grammar, and the other phonology item (Edmondson et al. 1992, downloaded, pp. 92-98) is an instrumental tone study silent on stress. Clouse 1997 (downloaded) independently states stress is non-contrastive across Lakes Plain. Nothing found suggests a different coding. sources.quote: 'stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date.' On Iau: 'Iau (Bateman 1990b, Edmonson et al. 1992) claims eight contrastive tones ... of the eight tones in Iau, four are short ... and the other four are nearly twice as long and occur on long (perhaps geminate?) vowels.'
